Within interior architecture education, anthropometry and ergonomics constitute foundational domains of knowledge for understanding the relationship between users and designed environments. Their pedagogical application often positions the user as a body to be measured, proportioned, and accommodated within space. This study recasts that initial framing by asking how these domains can be taught beyond the normative body and how they may support a relational understanding of user, action, object, and space. The study was conducted as part of an undergraduate course, Ergonomics in Interior Architecture, at Özyeğin University during the Fall 2024–2025 semester; through an active learning exercise structured around role-playing, a case study, and a poster session. The study was conducted in the Ergonomics in Interior Architecture course at Özyeğin University during the Fall 2024–2025 semester through an active learning exercise structured around role-playing, a case study, and a poster session. Students created fictional users with non-normative bodies, mapped their daily routines, and developed spatial and furniture proposals responsive to their abilities, limitations, and needs. The research material comprised the project posters and written reflections of 10 students who completed all stages of the exercise. The data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. The findings indicate that the students moved beyond the procedural application of anthropometric and ergonomic standards, interpreting bodily difference as a generator of design reasoning. The study suggests that by centering a non-normative user in a design problem, anthropometry and ergonomics can move beyond their conventional role as instruments of fit and become pedagogical means through which students learn to understand interior space as a relational field.

Robotic Surgical Systems (RSS) have fundamentally transformed modern clinical therapeutics by enabling unprecedented precision, minimally invasive dexterity, and enhanced 3D visualization. However, the convergence of complex mechatronics, autonomous software algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and telesurgery presents unprecedented regulatory, ethical, and clinical risk profiles. This comprehensive review provides a rigorous comparative analysis of global approval pathways across four major jurisdictions: the United States (FDA), the European Union (EU MDR), Japan (PMDA), and India (CDSCO). We examine pre-market medical device classification, substantial equivalence standards, clinical evaluation requirements, cyber-security paradigms, post-market surveillance (PMS), and surgeon credentialing compliance. Furthermore, this paper critically addresses emerging regulatory hurdles surrounding generative AI integration, autonomous robotic navigation, liabilities in telesurgical latency, and data privacy frameworks. Recommendations are offered for establishing globally harmonized regulatory standards and adaptive oversight protocols to safe-guard patient safety while fostering technological innovation.

A representative transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement system illustrates a high-risk structural-heart technology that enables replacement of the native tricuspid valve without conventional open-heart surgery. A system of this kind typically integrates a bovine-pericardial valve, a self-expanding nitinol frame and anchoring architecture, and a transfemoral venous delivery platform. Such devices have received Breakthrough Device designation and subsequent Premarket Approval (PMA) in the United States for patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) despite optimal medical therapy when replacement is deemed appropriate by a heart team. This article reconstructs the generalized regulatory journey for this device category and integrates classification, standards, clinical evidence, market positioning, global harmonization, project management, regulatory risk, human factors, quality systems, and real-world evidence. An illustrative Gantt chart provides a realistic development model for a device of this risk class. All budgets, schedules, and risk ratings presented are illustrative consultancy assumptions and are not drawn from any real company's internal records.Keywords: transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement; structural heart; Class III/IV medical device; Premarket Approval; Health Canada Class IV; project management; regulatory artificial intelligence

The empirical success of matrix-aware optimizers, such as Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) and Shampoo (arXiv:1802.09568), highlights the potential of non-Euclidean geometry for deep learning, including large language model (LLM) training. Despite this progress, the theoretical understanding of stochastic optimization in general normed spaces remains limited, particularly in distributed settings. We analyze minibatch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for smooth nonconvex optimization with respect to an arbitrary norm on a finite-dimensional space. Using the framework of $κ$-regular normed spaces (arXiv:0809.0813), we derive high-probability oracle complexity bounds under a light-tail condition stated directly in the dual norm induced by the update norm. The bounds make the dependence on geometry explicit through the regularity constant $κ$ of the dual space. In the Euclidean case, our bound recovers the standard minibatch SGD rate up to logarithmic factors. For some non-Euclidean geometries and noise models, it is sharper than bounds obtained by converting a Euclidean noise assumption, reducing a linear dimension dependence to a logarithmic one. Building on this framework, we introduce Rennala NSGD, a semi-asynchronous distributed algorithm, and establish wall-clock time complexity guarantees under fixed, heterogeneous worker computation times. In the Euclidean case ($κ=1$), our bound matches the parameter dependence of classical Rennala SGD up to logarithmic factors.

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has unsettled established assumptions in language education. For University Language Centres (LCs) and Self-Access Language Centres (SALCs), AI systems offering instant feedback, writing support, language models, and conversational practice raise questions about their distinctive institutional roles. This opinion paper argues that LCs and SALCs should not compete with AI as providers of content or feedback. Instead, they should become human-centred mediating institutions that help learners, teachers, and institutions use AI critically, ethically, and pedagogically. After revisiting their established roles in supporting autonomous and self-directed language learning, the paper argues that AI demands a more cautious understanding of autonomy, as apparent independence may conceal overreliance, weak evaluative judgement, and outsourced cognition (Barrett & Pack, 2023; Fan et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2024). It proposes five future functions of LCs and SALCs: AI literacy development, pedagogical curation, ethical mediation, reflective learner advising, and the integration of formal and informal learning. Drawing on the planned Language Education Institute at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, the paper illustrates how language policy, technology-enhanced pedagogy, and human-centred education may be aligned. Ultimately, the value of LCs and SALCs lies in cultivating judgement, agency, accountability, and community.

Aiming at the four prominent problems existing in current multi-process welding laboratories, including difficult supervision of teaching processes, high pressure on safety risk prevention and control, fragmented integration of teaching and management, and difficult implementation of intelligent transformation, this paper takes an eight-category multi-process, multi-equipment, and multi-scene welding experimental teaching system as the research object. Adopting the methods of literature research, field investigation, pilot verification and closed-loop optimization, this study constructs an integrated intelligent management system with in-depth integration of teaching and safety, covering the whole experimental process of pre-class, in-class and after-class stages supported by lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Lightweight AI capabilities are deeply embedded in four key links: standardization of teaching procedures, standardization of operational behaviors, evaluability of experimental quality, and early warning of safety risks, forming a low-cost, easy-to-implement, replicable and scalable intelligent management paradigm for engineering experiments. Practical results show that the proposed system significantly improves the standardization, proceduralization and objectivity of welding experimental teaching, strengthens the capabilities of pre-event early warning, rapid disposal and closed-loop rectification of safety risks, and effectively reduces human supervision omissions. It provides a referable practical path for the digital transformation of university experimental teaching and the modernization of laboratory governance capacity.

Amid rapid generative AI growth, cultivating AI literacy among non-computer science (non-CS) undergraduates is a key higher education reform priority. Drawing on national policies and domestic course experience, this study constructs a five-dimensional progressive AI literacy framework: fundamental knowledge, risk identification, safety awareness, ethical analysis, governance participation. Pedagogically, the course uses an online smart platform for multimodal delivery, case-based teaching, and integrated process-team assessment. In a teaching practice of AI Safety, Ethics, and Governance with 66 non-CS undergraduates (44 valid surveys), results show a moderate positive correlation between classroom interaction and team project quality; students highly value innovative assessments like team projects and self-designed questions, and most gain achievement from work selected as teaching cases. This study offers an empirically grounded, data-driven course design and evaluation framework, filling the general education gap for non-CS students.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in survey research, including to predict, simulate, or impute responses. Despite a rapidly growing interest in applications to create synthetic survey data, the empirical evidence remains fragmented, with substantial variation in research objectives, model architectures, ``persona'' construction strategies, and validation practices. This paper presents a systematic review of 55 studies published between 2022 and 2025 that use LLMs to generate, predict, or impute responses in survey and related attitudinal or behavioral data. The results suggest that LLM-based survey simulation is best understood as a conditional, use-case-specific tool rather than a general substitute for traditional imputation methods and human respondents. We outline concrete steps toward a more coherent evaluation framework, including use-case-specific metric selection, relational alignment as a standard validity check, and greater transparency in model and design choices.

ResearchMind AI is an AI-powered system designed to simplify research paper analysis across multiple domains. It enables users to upload and analyze multiple research papers in PDF format. PyMuPDF is used to extract text, while Sentence Transformers generate semantic embeddings. ChromaDB stores and retrieves relevant information through semantic search. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is integrated with an open-source Large Language Model (LLM) to provide context-based answers. The system supports automated literature survey generation, research gap identification, paper comparison, and intelligent question answering. It also generates structured research reports summarizing key findings and future research directions. The application uses React.js for the frontend and Flask with Python for the backend. ResearchMind AI aims to reduce manual effort, improve research organization, and make literature analysis more efficient.

Over the last decade, industrial systems have been shaken by overlapping crises such as climate change, pandemics, resource pressures, and geopolitical instability. In response, Industry 5.0 has moved beyond the automation-centered logic of Industry 4.0 by placing human well-being, sustainability, and resilience at the core of industrial value creation. In parallel, circular-economy thinking encourages firms to redesign supply chains around closed material loops, extended product lifetimes, and higher-value resource recovery. This chapter examines how Industry 5.0 and the circular economy can mutually reinforce each other when supported by digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, blockchain, and digital twins. Rather than being treated as purely technical add-ons, these technologies enable predictive risk management, real-time monitoring, improved traceability, and more adaptive supply-chain configurations. Drawing on illustrative cases from the automotive, electronics, fashion, food and beverage, and logistics sectors, the chapter demonstrates that human-centered governance is a key condition for translating digital and circular strategies into resilient supply-chain practices. It concludes by proposing a human-centric circular resilience framework that positions resilience and risk management as central mechanisms for sustainable resource valorization and outlines implications for policymakers, industrial practitioners, and researchers.

documents.abstract: Introduction Despite growing recognition that resilience and work engagement are central to employee wellbeing, the mechanisms through which resilience is associated with engaged work behaviour remain underexplored. Grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined task, cognitive, and relational job crafting as parallel mediating mechanisms in the resilience-work engagement relationship. Methods Cross-sectional data were collected from 332 employees at a large financial services organisation operating across South Africa and Namibia. Resilience, job crafting, and work engagement were assessed using validated measures. A parallel mediation model was tested using PROCESS macro Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results Resilience significantly predicted all three crafting behaviours and work engagement. All indirect effects were statistically significant. Cognitive crafting showed the largest estimated indirect effect, followed by relational and task crafting. The model explained 34% of variance in work engagement, with crafting behaviours accounting for approximately 45% of the total effect of resilience on engagement. The direct effect remained significant, indicating partial mediation. Discussion Resilient employees actively reshape their work through behavioural, cognitive, and relational crafting, and this proactive activity meaningfully explains how resilience generates engagement. Cognitive reframing of work as purposeful and meaningful emerged as the most potent pathway. Findings carry practical relevance for resilience training, leadership practice, and organisational job design.

documents.abstract: Background: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems move from supply chain decision support towards operational execution, governance must distinguish technical capability from permissible decision authority. This study develops a reversibility-aware framework for allocating human–AI control according to decision risk, recoverability, uncertainty and consequence propagation.Methods: A design science research-inspired approach was used to operationalise four constructs on normalised scales and integrate them into an equally weighted Decision Control Score (DCS), supplemented by governance overrides. Five control modes, from HC-0 (human-controlled) to HC-4 (monitored AI execution), were evaluated using six author-constructed supply chain scenarios. The framework was compared with illustrative fixed HC-3 and risk-only baselines, followed by reversibility and weighting sensitivity analyses.Results: The framework assigned HC-4 to routine inventory replenishment, HC-3 to forecast adjustment and purchase-order quantity modification, HC-2 to logistics rerouting, HC-1 to supplier selection or replacement, and HC-0 to critical supply interruption response. Its recommendations differed from the risk-only baseline in two of six scenarios. When the other constructs were held constant, varying reversibility changed the logistics-rerouting control mode. Across four alternative weighting configurations and six scenarios, 23 of 24 classifications matched the equal-weight results (95.8%).Conclusion: The analytical evaluation illustrates how recovery feasibility can affect rule-based control allocation. Because scenario inputs, weights, thresholds and safeguards were stipulated rather than empirically calibrated, these findings do not establish operational effectiveness or predictive validity. Independent expert assessment and field validation are required before implementation.

documents.abstract: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have evolved from primarily cartographic and spatial-data management environments into core analytical infrastructure for water-resource engineering. Their application now spans watershed delineation, rainfall–runoff modelling, groundwater assessment, flood and drought analysis, irrigation planning, water-quality assessment, river management and water-distribution infrastructure. However, the literature is fragmented across application domains and frequently attributes the predictive capability of remote sensing, hydrological models or machine-learning algorithms to GIS itself. This review critically synthesizes the evidence contained in a 20-study working corpus and supplements it with recent peer-reviewed literature to identify how GIS contributes to water-resource engineering, where its contribution is strongest, and which methodological weaknesses continue to limit transferability and decision reliability. The review is organized around six application domains and evaluates the GIS role across data integration, terrain analysis, spatial modelling, decision support, visualization and model coupling. The synthesis shows a transition from conventional GIS-based watershed and groundwater mapping toward integrated workflows combining digital elevation models, satellite observations, hydrological/hydraulic models, geostatistics, artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Nevertheless, recurring weaknesses are evident: non-reproducible literature selection, inconsistent validation, inadequate uncertainty quantification, scale mismatch, dependence on subjective weighting in multi-criteria methods, insufficient benchmarking between GIS-enabled and non-GIS workflows, and geographical concentration of evidence.Recent systematic reviews reinforce these concerns, particularly the need for standardized validation and uncertainty protocols and for multi-source, physically informed modelling. The review therefore proposes a GIS–water-resource engineering framework in which GIS is treated not as the predictive model itself but as the spatial integration and decision-support layer connecting observations, process models, data-driven models and management actions. A research agenda is proposed around uncertainty-aware GIS, hybrid physics–AI modelling, cloud-native geospatial workflows, real-time sensor integration, digital twins, explainable AI and reproducible open science. The review provides a conceptual basis for researchers and practitioners to design more transparent, validated and decision-oriented GIS applications in water-resource engineering.

This paper examines the limitations of artificial intelligence–driven managerial rationality in top management, with a focus on agent-based AI models. This study employs a systematic literature review using a PRISMA-inspired approach to analyze agent-based AI models in executive decision-making contexts. Drawing on the contemporary scientific literature, the study conceptualizes AI as a probabilistic decision-support mechanism rather than an autonomous managerial actor. The paper identifies key structural and epistemic constraints of agent-based AI, including probabilistic outputs, bounded rationality, and contextual dependence, emphasizing the need for sustained human participation and oversight in executive decision-making.

documents.abstract: The increasing integration of GenAI into academic writing has prompted renewed attention to how students engage with writing tasks in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) contexts. While existing research has focused on GenAI's capabilities and risks, it has paid less attention to the instructional conditions that shape how students use these tools. This paper proposes the Rigor–Commitment Alignment Framework (RCAF), a conceptual model that examines the interaction between academic rigor and teacher commitment as two dimensions of the pedagogical environment. Drawing on research in academic literacies, engagement theory, self-determination theory, and visible learning, the framework identifies four instructional configurations (Neglectful, Indulgent, Punitive, and Rigor with Support) and links them, through a set of testable propositions, to four engagement profiles (deep-agentic, strategic, surface, and disengaged). The framework is grounded in Bandura’s (1986) triadic reciprocal model, in which personal factors, observable behavior, and the instructional environment reciprocally influence one another. The analysis suggests that patterns of GenAI use cannot be understood solely in terms of technological affordances, and may be substantially shaped by the interaction between task demands, teacher commitment, and student engagement. In this context, GenAI may either support higher-order academic literacy practices or facilitate low-effort task completion, depending on the alignment between rigor and commitment. The RCAF provides a conceptual basis for examining these dynamics and offers implications for EAP pedagogy and AI policy.

Ensuring business continuity in critical cyber–physical infrastructures requires a holistic risk management approach that anticipates, quantifies, and controls complex cascading effects across interdependent services. This chapter presents the solution approach developed by the DYNABIC project, which pivots around RISKM4BC , a reusable methodology and supporting tools to manage risks that affect business continuity. The approach integrates: (i) a Bow-tie Smart Center that structures threats, barriers, and consequences and is augmented with information from Large Language Models (LLMs) to enrich scenario coverage and generate mitigation recommendations; (ii) predictive business process monitoring that forecasts the performance and risk of incident response workflows; and (iii) a cascading risk model that, based on Bayesian networks, quantifies interdependent risk exposure and updates it in near real time when new evidence arrives. The methodology is operationalized through traceable risk profiles and goal-oriented aggregation that align model outputs with business objectives, as well as through user-facing views that connect live evidence to decisions. A high-level architecture describes how these components interact with monitoring and digital-twin data to maintain a live risk picture for decision making of both human operators and automated responses. A running example from transportation infrastructure (by Ferrovial) illustrates how the methodology produces actionable risk alerts (e.g., congestion likelihood and business impact level), anticipates resolution timelines, and evaluates exposure to external dependencies (e.g., power or communications). We conclude the description of the approach with methodological advantages, lessons learned, and future extensions, including business-goal linking, automated incident reporting, and interactive what-if analysis.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often conditioned into specific roles such as tutors, interviewers, or agents acting for an organisation, through system prompts that specify how they should behave. The extent to which they can actually adhere to these role specifications under multi-turn interactions with realistic and potentially problematic users is understudied. To address this, we propose user behaviour fuzzing, a guided search over plausible user behaviours that can lead a model to violate its role specification, and introduce RoleFUZZER, a framework that adapts coverage-guided fuzzing from software testing to operationalise the search. RoleFUZZER constructs scenarios guided by a user-behaviour coverage grid that crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types and the role specification of the model under test i.e. what is under pressure. With RoleFUZZER, we evaluate LLMs across five role specifications, including tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and web agent under organisational policies. Across simulated and validated conversations in 15 campaigns, the framework reaches >= 89% coverage of the 64-cell behaviour grid for every model and role tested, and surfaces specification-grounded failure patterns. At an equal budget of conversations, removing the RoleFUZZER grid and asking an LLM to generate specification targeting users free-form lowers coverage to 39-69% with fewer kinds of violations. The same specification can also fail in opposite directions. For e.g., on the antagonist, open-weight target models override the player's safety signals, while Claude Haiku 4.5 breaks character instead. RoleFUZZER offers a tractable way to uncover vulnerabilities in LLMs across role specifications by testing diverse user behaviours that are likely to violate them.

documents.abstract: Agents deployed at scale repeatedly encounter related problems, and it is natural to let them learn from each other's experience rather than starting over each time. Unfortunately, there is no single way to retain that experience that works well across settings, and no way to know in advance which future problems a given experience will help with. A global history preserves every detail but becomes expensive and mixes together experience that may not belong together; compressing that history into one fixed representation limits the cost but can throw away valuable details. We introduce Routed Continual Learning (Routed CL), an architecture that decides how to partition and retain experience. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, each of which maintains state using one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM-based router either reuses an existing cluster or creates a new one, basing its decision on the problem statement, memory system descriptions, and cluster summaries. We also introduce Context Memory Adapter, which mediates between the memory system and the agentic loop. We evaluate the architecture on a heterogeneous stream that interleaves 301 instances from the six CL-Bench tasks with 97 banking instances from $τ^3$-Bench. Across four language models and five matched rollouts, Routed Continual Learning raises normalized reward over a single global in-context learning (ICL) history by 15-30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward, achieves higher mean normalized reward than ICL-only clustering, and reduces estimated API cost by 65-72% relative to Global ICL. These results support approaching continual learning as a routing problem that chooses both a learning mechanism and a state cluster rather than committing to one representation globally.

Rubrics enable reward assignment on tasks without verifiable answers, but are expensive to manually produce from scratch. We present Rubricon, a pipeline that generates discriminative rubrics without requiring human preference labels, rubric annotation, or generator-model training. Using any LLM, Rubricon samples multiple rubrics, selects the most discriminative candidate, adds criteria to capture overlooked requirements or response flaws, and prunes criteria that are misaligned or shallow. Alongside LLM self-critique and test-time scaling, Rubricon uses observed criterion pass rates on example model responses to guide refinement. Across five professional, consumer, clinical, and general-use LLM benchmarks, Rubricon produces rubrics whose scores of frontier LLM responses exhibit 9% greater alignment with labor-intensive expert-authored rubrics, compared to the best alternative synthetic rubric generation method among RRD, QSRG, OpenRubrics, and agentic generation via harnesses like Codex. On HealthBench, post-training a Qwen3.5-9B model with Rubricon rubrics yields 4.5% better performance than training with rubrics from the strongest alternative synthetic rubric generator, RRD.

documents.abstract: This chapter explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated dialogic reflection as a transformative scaffold for teacher inquiry and professional learning. While reflective practice is widely recognized as foundational to teacher development, contemporary educational contexts often reduce it to solitary, checklist-driven compliance that prioritizes polished outputs over meaningful sense-making. Drawing on sociocultural theory and dialogic pedagogy, the chapter conceptualizes reflection as a socially mediated, inquiry-oriented process through which language teachers co-construct professional knowledge by engaging with multiple voices, including peers, mentors, students, academic research and classroom evidence. The chapter synthesizes research on dialogic reflection, teacher inquiry and technology-enhanced professional learning to show that reflection becomes transformative only when it is intentionally scaffolded, ethically grounded and oriented toward questioning rather than closure. Building on this foundation, the chapter examines how digital technologies and generative AI in particular can expand dialogic spaces across time and contexts. Rather than positioning AI as an authoritative source of answers, the chapter frames it as a nonauthoritative dialogic partner that supports noticing, provokes reflection, and sustains reflective continuity. The chapter concludes by proposing principled design guidelines for AI-mediated dialogic reflection that prioritize teacher agency, relational ethics, and research-oriented professionalism within broader human dialogic ecologies.

Purpose This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is perceived as a decision-support mechanism in school principals’ decision-making, focusing on its perceived implications for decisional capital within a centralized education system. Design/methodology/approach Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 17 public school principals across different school levels in Türkiye. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify how GenAI is interpreted and positioned within principals’ decision-making processes. Findings Principals reported decision-making challenges driven by bureaucratic procedures, restricted autonomy and competing stakeholder demands. Within these constraints, GenAI was seen not as a substitute for professional judgment but as cognitive support that may improve access to information, facilitate scenario-based reasoning and inform evidence-based judgments. Principals reported varying levels of readiness to integrate GenAI into organizational decision-making, with this variation associated with digital competence, institutional support and ethical awareness. Originality/value The study extends discussions of principals’ decision-making by linking GenAI-enabled decision support to the exercise of decisional capital under centralized governance constraints, highlighting conditions under which GenAI may contribute to human-centered and ethically grounded organizational decision-making processes.

Landslides remain one of the most frequent and destructive natural hazards globally, significantly influenced by climate change, rapid urbanization, deforestation, and unplanned developmental activities. In response, geospatial technologies such as Remote Sensing (RS), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and machine learning techniques have increasingly been applied to improve landslide prediction, monitoring, susceptibility mapping, and disaster risk reduction. This study presents a bibliometric evaluation of global research trends related to geospatial technologies in landslide studies during the period 2000–2025. A total of 14,909 publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus were analysed using the bibliometrix package in R. The analysis identified 2,385 publication sources and an annual scientific growth rate of 14.64%, indicating the rapid expansion of research activities in the field. The study examined publication trends, citation impact, thematic evolution, keyword structure, and international collaboration patterns. The results revealed substantial growth in scientific production, particularly after 2018, driven by advances in spatial data acquisition, artificial intelligence integration, and increasing global disaster risk awareness. China, Italy, India, and the United States emerged as the leading contributors to the research domain. Keyword and thematic analyses demonstrated a clear transition from conventional geomorphological and mapping-based approaches toward advanced machine learning-driven predictive modelling and geospatial monitoring frameworks. The study further identified two major interconnected research streams: remote sensing-based monitoring and GIS-based susceptibility modelling. The findings highlight the growing global significance, interdisciplinary nature, and technological advancement of geospatial applications in landslide research and disaster management.

Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides coarse supervision for long-horizon LLM agents: failed trajectories may contain correct steps, while successful trajectories can contain errors. Trajectory-level skills can also shift teacher preferences at unrelated steps, introducing off-target distillation signals. We introduce SCOPE, a framework for Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation. After a supervised warm-up, the policy analyzes its own trajectories, generates step-specific hindsight skills, and distills their guidance only at selected error steps. A bounded signed teacher-student coefficient stabilizes auxiliary updates while preserving positive reinforcement and negative correction. A success-relative pairwise length reward further encourages efficient task completion. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple model backbones. With Qwen2.5-3B, SCOPE achieves 97.7% success on ALFWorld and 85.2% on WebShop, outperforming SEED by 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE reaches 89.6% success, improving over GRPO by 23.2 percentage points with 46.7% fewer interactions. Scaling to Qwen3-32B, SCOPE achieves 99.2% success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 94.0% on unseen tasks.

The acquisition of English as a second language (L2) is increasingly shaped by rapidly changing educational, social, technological, and digital environments, particularly in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). This study investigates the acquisition of English as a second language from the perspectives of students, teachers, and parents, with particular attention to the dynamic interaction of individual, familial, classroom, and technological factors. Guided by Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), the study conceptualizes English language acquisition as a dynamic and interconnected process that develops through the continuous interaction of multiple contextual and individual variables. A case-study research design was employed, and purposive sampling was used to select participants from Punjab, Pakistan. The study comparatively examines patterns of convergence and divergence across these three stakeholder perspectives to develop a multidimensional understanding of English L2 acquisition in the contemporary AI-mediated learning environment. Its practical implications extend to students, parents, teachers, educational institutions, policymakers, curriculum developers, and teacher-education programmes by informing the development of more responsive and technology-integrated approaches to English language learning. Furthermore, the findings may provide insights for AI and NLP developers, digital learning designers, social-media platforms, and digital content creators to develop linguistically accessible, learner-centred, and context-sensitive English-learning resources. Overall, the study seeks to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of how multiple stakeholders perceive and experience English L2 acquisition in an increasingly AI-driven educational landscape.

Critical Infrastructures (CIs) are increasingly complex cyber-physical systems whose interdependencies expose societies to cascading failures triggered by cyber and physical threats. Traditional risk assessment methods and intrusion detection systems are insufficient to address rare, high-impact, and unforeseen attacks, highlighting the need for resilience-oriented approaches that extend beyond prevention. This chapter presents AWARE4BC, a framework developed within the DYNABIC initiative to enhance CI resilience and business continuity through Digital Twin–enabled services. AWARE4BC integrates continuous infrastructure monitoring, advanced attack and anomaly detection, and holistic resilience assessment based on runtime observations. It leverages heterogeneous data sources, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and semantically enriched threat indicators to support real-time situational awareness and evidence-based decision-making. Resilience is quantified through effectiveness and resilience curves capturing degradation, absorption, recovery, and adaptation across multiple concerns, including technical, economic, environmental, and social dimensions. The framework’s practicality is validated through a hackathon-based evaluation using a transportation use case, demonstrating its ability to detect both known and zero-day attacks and assess their cascading impacts. Results confirm the added value of combining security monitoring with resilience assessment. AWARE4BC offers a generic, modular approach applicable across CI domains, contributing to more robust and adaptive protection of essential services.

The purpose of this study is to evaluate and prioritize next-generation artificial intelligence (AI) technologies for sustainable pharmaceutical supply chains by considering multiple technological, operational, sustainability, and regulatory criteria. Within the methodology of the study, an integrated LOPCOW–RAFSI multi-criteria decision-making framework was employed. Fifteen evaluation criteria were identified through a comprehensive literature review and reviewed for domain relevance and applicability, and six AI technology alternatives—Generative AI, Agentic AI, AI-powered Digital Twin, Federated Learning, Explainable AI, and Reinforcement Learning—were evaluated. The LOPCOW method was used to determine objective criterion weights, while the RAFSI method was applied to rank the alternatives. The findings indicate that AI-powered Digital Twin (A3) achieved the highest RAFSI score (0.666060), followed by Agentic AI (A2) (0.547032) and Explainable AI (A5) (0.541363), resulting in the overall ranking A3 > A2 > A5 > A6 > A4 > A1. The sensitivity analysis further showed that A3 retained the first position across all examined scenarios (S0–S6), although limited rank reversals occurred between A2 and A5. As a contribution to the literature, this study integrates objective weighting and robust ranking within a unified decision-support framework for evaluating emerging AI technologies and provides decision-makers with a systematic and transparent basis for prioritizing AI investments in sustainable pharmaceutical supply chains.

documents.abstract: The optimal artificial intelligence model for imputing missing wave observation data may vary according to the physical characteristics of the target variable and the missingness pattern. This study compared a temporal model, SAITS, with spatiotemporal models, GRIN, SPIN, and ImputeFormer, using 30-min interval wave observations from five stations along the southeastern coast of Korea. All models were evaluated under identical data, data-splitting, sequence, and masking conditions. Performance differences and statistical ties between model pairs were assessed using window-level paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. In an evaluation in which the final time step at the target station was artificially masked, SAITS yielded the lowest errors for significant wave height and significant wave period, whereas SPIN achieved the lowest angular error for wave direction, a circular variable. In the missingness-pattern sensitivity experiments, performance differences among models were generally small across random missingness rates. In contrast, under contiguous missingness within a window, GRIN achieved the best performance for both significant wave height and significant wave period when the missingness rate was at least 20%, exhibiting a pattern distinct from that observed under random missingness. Notably, under 50% contiguous missingness, GRIN was the only deep learning model that produced lower errors than linear interpolation for both significant wave height and significant wave period. These findings indicate that imputation performance may be more sensitive to the temporal continuity of missing values than to the overall missingness rate. They further suggest that exploiting spatiotemporal dependencies can be effective for reconstructing consecutive missing segments, particularly when the contiguous missingness rate exceeds 20%.

AI-assisted procurement combines supplier observations, product matching, cost estimates and human judgments. This working paper examines how evidence, advisory outputs, eligibility checks and permission to act can be separated. A retrospective documentary case from QuickAIBuy motivates a proposed control architecture and a reproducible Boolean counterexample. Exhaustive enumeration finds advisory-dependent permission changes in three of eight paired comparisons under the deliberately coupled rule and zero under the separated rule. These are properties of an illustrative model, not measured procurement outcomes. A synthetic supplier-quote example, implementation test plan and reusable buyer review card translate the analysis into practical checks. Scope: author-approved working paper, not peer reviewed. Historical internal records were not independently rerun; no customer outcomes or production safety are established. ChatGPT assisted with synthesis, drafting, diagrams and model construction, as disclosed in the manuscript. Mohammad Maani approved the content and public deposit on 28 October 2026. Affiliation and project context: https://www.quickaibuy.com Included materials: manuscript PDF, standalone Python reproducibility script and Boolean truth-table CSV.

documents.abstract: Precision medicine hopes to make health care better by accounting for the variability of individuals' biology and clinical features in disease prediction and treatment. To achieve personalized care, however, it is essential that sex- and gender-related factors are recognized as they impact the mechanisms of disease, pharmacological actions and clinical outcomes. Disease susceptibility and response to treatment may differ between the sexes due to sex-related differences in genetics, hormones, immune regulation, epigenetic processes and metabolism; and diagnosis, access to healthcare, use of treatment and outcome may also differ across sex. There is growing evidence that considers sex and gender aspects in pharmacotherapy, discovery of biomarkers, artificial intelligence and multi-omics. Although this is starting to be recognized, there are still limitations of representation in clinical research, inconsistencies in how it is reported, and a lack of translation to clinical applications. This narrative review discusses the latest evidence regarding sex and gender differences in disease biology, pharmacotherapy, and clinical outcomes and their potential contribution to precision medicine. The incorporation of these factors into personalized health care systems can improve risk stratification, optimization of therapy, safety of drugs, and patient care.

Geospatial target localization refers to determining the geographic location of targets from natural language queries, which is essential for applications such as urban management, emergency response, and location-based services. As user queries evolve from address matching toward complex forms incorporating multiple spatial semantic factors, the localization process increasingly demands the coordination of heterogeneous tools and data sources. Automation remains hindered by the lack of a unified structured representation for semantic factors, the difficulty of translating complex spatial constraints into executable operations, and the unreliability of single-round planning and execution. This study proposes SGTAgent, an agent framework for geospatial target localization from complex spatial semantic queries. The parser transforms queries into structured spatial semantic factors, the planner organizes dependent spatial workflows, and the feedback mechanism distinguishes local parameter refinement from workflow restructuring. Experiments show that SGTAgent achieves higher localization accuracy than the evaluated generic baselines across multiple LLM backbones. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, SGTAgent achieves localization accuracies of 39.86%, 68.76%, and 81.88% at distance thresholds of 100, 300, and 500 m, respectively, outperforming the evaluated agents under the corresponding experimental configurations. On complex queries using GPT-4o, it achieves an LA@500m of 80.47%, compared with 70.12% for ReAct. Ablation experiments show that removing the complete Restate–Replan feedback mechanism reduces the 500 m localization accuracy from 81.88% to 74.83%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the execution feedback mechanism under the evaluated configuration. An independent evaluation of the parser achieves macro-F1 scores of 89.76% on the original benchmark and 89.62% on independently formulated queries, indicating consistent semantic factor extraction capability across different query formulations.

This systematic review and meta -analysis estimated the prevalence of sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers (HWW) and evaluated hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination coverage and HBV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, SciELO, the Virtual Health Library, the CAPES Periodicals Portal, and Google Scholar were searched through 19 May 2026. Twenty-two studies involving approximately 9,000 HWW and 1,722 sharps injuries were included. Random-effects meta -analyses used logit transformation and restricted maximum likelihood estimation. The pooled prevalence of sharps injuries was 34.1% (95% CI, 22.8–47.5%), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.9%). HBV vaccination coverage was 31.1% (95% CI, 8.2–68.3%) and was not associated with sharps injury prevalence (β = 0.338; p = 0.544). Pooled HBV and HCV prevalence estimates were 2.3% (95% CI, 0.3–15.4%) and 3.36% (95% CI, 1.17–9.23%), respectively. No HCV seroconversion was reported in follow-up studies. Approximately one-third of HWW experienced sharps injuries, highlighting the need to strengthen waste segregation, personal protective equipment use, biosafety training, HBV vaccination, and occupational surveillance to improve worker safety and reduce preventable blood-borne infections.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Skills-based organizing replaces jobs and credentials with information on skills, which artificial intelligence now extracts from job postings, résumés and human resource records at scale. Whether this information is valid for the decisions it supports depends on whether research on skills intelligence and research on human resource management inform each other. We mapped 3649 documents published between 2000 and 2026, screened with a large language model audited against a human reviewer, using co-citation, bibliographic coupling and permutation benchmarks. Managerial and computational research form separate communities: only 13% of coupling links connect them, against 46% expected by chance, and the divide is sharpest between studies of the same practice, recruitment and selection. Computational research, 71% of output in 2023–2025, is itself split between recruitment technology and labor-market analytics; it validates skill information mainly against annotated text, about one study in seven relates it to outcomes, and almost none evaluates the decisions it informs. Taxonomies such as ESCO and O*NET do not bridge the communities; work analysis does. We propose a skills intelligence value chain from data to outcomes, with five testable propositions and a research agenda for validating AI-produced skill information.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

documents.abstract: Modern societies increasingly rely on critical infrastructures powered by the Internet of Things (IoT), Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), and the Digital Twin (DT) paradigm. However, their distributed and heterogeneous nature presents complex security challenges across devices, networks, and third-party integrations. This chapter introduces Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response for Business Continuity (SOAR4BC)—a core service within the DT framework designed to safeguard such infrastructures. SOAR4BC integrates Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and SOAR principles to select and execute optimal security workflows dynamically. When human oversight is needed, Chat4Operator facilitates interaction, allowing operators to approve, modify, or request alternatives. We validate SOAR4BC through real-world use cases, demonstrating its reliability and adaptability. This work highlights the potential of combining DT, DRL, and large language models (LLMs) to enhance security orchestration in IoT/CPS environments.

The convergence of smart tourism technologies and social media platforms has fundamentally transformed the way travelers plan, experience, and share their journeys. This chapter examines the intersection of smart tourism ecosystems and social media dynamics through a performative travel lens, exploring how digital platforms shape tourist behavior, destination image, and the co-creation of travel experiences. Drawing on performance theory, digital sociology, and smart tourism frameworks, this chapter analyzes how it influences both individual travel decisions and broader destination marketing strategies. Smart technologies such as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, big data analytics, and augmented reality are explored for their role in enabling personalized, immersive, and socially mediated tourism experiences. This chapter ultimately argues that the future of smart tourism lies not only in technological advancement but in the thoughtful integration of digital tools with human-centered, socially conscious travel values.

Interdisciplinary teams play a central role in solving complex scientific and operational problems, yet they frequently struggle to collaborate effectively despite high levels of technical expertise. These breakdowns often stem not only from knowledge gaps but also from difficulties interpreting collaborators’ assumptions, reasoning processes, and disciplinary perspectives. Although research on shared mental models emphasizes the importance of aligned team knowledge structures, the social-cognitive mechanisms that enable such alignment remain poorly specified. This paper argues that social perspective taking (SPT) is a foundational but under examined process linking individual understanding to team cognition. We bring together concepts from across multiple disciplines to propose a multilevel framework that reconceptualizes perspective taking as an emergent team process shaped by contextual conditions, motivational and feedback mechanisms, and interactional practices.

With the rapid uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, academic risks need to be viewed as not only technical issues but as socio-institutional harms that impact equity, trust, and accountability. The methodology used for this study is a conceptual literature review and qualitative synthesis of existing academic research. This study tackles the problem existing in the literature, which is unstructured definitions, by synthesizing the literature to create a complete conceptual framework for Social Risk Management (SRM). The proposed framework places SRM in a unique role, serving as the institutional interface between the introduction of AI and social outcomes, with the role of a mediator and moderator between the raw technical inputs and the negative effects of AI on society. There are four main operational pillars of SRM identified in the synthesis. This study also adds the competency of SRM as a core competency of governance, not only for its ethical dimension but also for being a proactive competency. Moreover, it offers a clear research program for future empirical studies, detailing potential ways to measure SRM and to investigate its differences in various application areas of universities, such as admissions, financial aid, tutoring, and even assessment.

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explain how socio-economic wellness can become a repeatable organisational capability through participatory diagnosis, negotiated work redesign, hidden-cost translation and socio-financial governance. Design/methodology/approach A theory-building integrative review combines SEAM with organisational wellness and intervention, job-design and motivation, internal branding, equity and capability literatures. The synthesis is mechanism-based and literature-only; no company-level evidence is analysed. Findings Socio-economic wellness capability is defined as the patterned ability to detect, discuss, correct and monitor work-system dysfunctions affecting employee experience and organisational performance. The four interdependent mechanisms are conditioned by voice safety, managerial authority and resources, resource pressure, equity and governance continuity. Research limitations/implications The framework is conceptual and requires longitudinal, comparative and mixed-method testing. Future studies can operationalise its mechanisms and boundary conditions across sectors and institutional contexts. Practical implications Managers should assess wellness through operating routines: who can surface dysfunctions, whether diagnosis leads to authorised redesign, whether human consequences enter socio-economic evidence, and whether governance forums sustain learning. Social implications The framework highlights equitable access to organisational voice and influence over work conditions, extending wellness beyond programme access. Originality/value The paper differentiates socio-economic wellness capability from programmes, well-being states and organisational-health perspectives. It offers a bounded mechanism-based account of how work-system knowledge becomes authorised correction, socio-economic prioritisation and recurrent governance learning.

This article proposes socio-techno-ecological imaginaries (STEI) as a conceptual extension of sociotechnical imaginaries (STI). While STI has been valuable for showing how social order and technological change co-produce “desirable futures,” we argue it tends to leave implicit how visions of ecology – beliefs about what nature is and acts, how it is valued, and how humans ought to relate to it – are entangled in this process. This implicitness risks limiting STI’s explanatory power, its capacity to evaluate the desirability of imagined futures amid socio-ecological crises, and its own imaginative horizon in futures work. Drawing on literatures on socio-ecological imagination, eco-social imaginaries, and environmental and nature imaginaries, we define STEIs as institutionally embedded and publicly performed visions of desirable futures, animated by specific understandings and valuations of society, technology and ecology. STEI rests on three premises: (1) imaginaries are co-produced across social, technical, and ecological dimensions; (2) each dimension carries specific assumptions and normative valuations that condition what futures are deemed plausible and desirable; and (3) alignment or misalignment across these assumptions and valuations can be sites of conflict, lock-in, and transformation. We demonstrate the framework’s analytical value through an empirical study of the STEIs that guide the development and use expectations of sensor technologies in the Dutch agricultural sector. The study combines interviews with a corpus of public web texts to identify two STEIs, showing how divergent visions of society, technology, and ecology co-produce distinct farming futures. STEI, we conclude, strengthens critical futures research by enabling more explicit, plural, and ecologically attuned evaluations of future-making.

Executive Abstract: This paper examines multi-dialect stress-testing of enterprise language systems, the cross-border privacy boundarybetween Saudi PDPL, Moroccan Law 09-08 (CNDP), and European processing, and the human-oversight duties that EU AI Act Article 4 and Annex III (Section 3) place on institutional deployers. Standard English-to-Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) benchmarks mask severe operational failures when conversational agents and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines encounter authentic intra-prompt code-switching (Moroccan Darija + French, Saudi Najdi/Gulf + English, Egyptian, and Levantine). Evaluating 7 foundation models against the Arabic AI Observatory v2.0 Master Corpus (521 deterministic adversarial scenarios), we document a 37.0% accuracy degradation under dialectal negation shifts, a 2.41x token fertility infrastructure tax (1.18 vs. 2.85 tokens/word), and critical cross-border PII exfiltration vulnerabilities. Finally, we specify a zero-knowledge SHA-256 provenance protocol anchored on WaqfLedger.tech.
