documents.abstract: Spectroscopic diagnostics provide rich information for characterizing plasma states in tokamak fusion experiments, while existing learning-based approaches are often designed for individual tasks and rely heavily on labeled data. In this work, we propose SpectralTF-MAE, a self-supervised spectral foundation model for tokamak plasma diagnostics. The model is pretrained on paired charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) and X-ray crystal spectroscopy (XCS) measurements through masked spectral reconstruction. To better capture diagnostically important spectral structures, we introduce a peak-aware masking strategy together with a peak-enhanced reconstruction objective, encouraging the model to focus on characteristic spectral regions. A shared Transformer encoder is employed to learn transferable representations across different diagnostic modalities. The pretrained model is further adapted to several downstream tasks, including plasma-parameter prediction, cross-diagnostic spectral generation, and spectral peak analysis. Experiments on EAST diagnostic data demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance across different tasks and consistently benefits from self-supervised spectral pretraining. These results indicate the potential of SpectralTF-MAE as a general and transferable representation learning framework for plasma spectroscopic diagnostics.

Abstract AI systems increasingly serve as social partners, companions, and romantic partners, yet governance remains fragmented, reactive, and split between clinical applications and anthropomorphic deception. Current Canadian AI regulation (PIPEDA and the un-proclaimed AIDA) addresses privacy and market access only, while Character.AI and a growing list of anthropomorphic-chatbot suicide cases point directly to the product-liability question that no Canadian instrument answers. This gap illustrates the regulatory break that motivates this paper. In the physcial world, the ethics → policy → engineering loop (EPE loop) works as a mutually protective cycle in which ethics specifies the values a system must serve, engineering builds mechanisms that support them, and policy verifies and enforces them, so that companies and stakeholders share benefits from a standardized technique world. Virtual AI services and products, however, do not inherit that protection. Their values are relational, their mechanisms conversational, and their harms uncodified, so the EPE loop does not close. This systematic review of 169 studies examines where the loop breaks. This systematic review examines how engineering, ethics, and policy shape human-AI relationships between 2022-2026 and identifies challenges and opportunities at their intersections. Following PRISMA 2020, seven databases yielded 395 records; 169 studies met inclusion criteria. Reflexive Thematic Analysis and K-means clustering synthesized our findings. We identify three distinct clusters. The empirical group (n = 30) is characterized by empirical research that documents deception and vulnerability but lacks governance support, producing a regulatory gap. The anthropomorphism group (n = 83) focuses on engagement and safety, and is characterized by the highest standardization gaps that is mostly implicit stated, meaning researchers name the harms but never specify the technique standards against which those harms would be measured. The clinical group (n = 56) shows strong policy engagement but the largest conceptual framing gap, and its high principle-to-practice gap indicates that the gap becomes visible precisely because its principles are codified, yet the cluster lacks broad conceptual exploration of additional missing values such as relational and communicative harms. We show that the three governance failures are three skipped Value-Senstive-Design (VSD) obligations: technical (Cluster 1), conceptual (Cluster 2), and empirical-to-instrument (Cluster 0). We propose a research agenda that closes each gap. For anthropomorphic AI, technique solutions developed into technical standards; for highly regulated domains, broader conceptual maps of the values they have not yet admitted; and, across all three clusters, stakeholder-anchored empirical work under VSD framework. We further argue that VSD values are not exhausted by design values but include ethical values and, potentially, policy values, which is what allows the EPE loop to rotate again. So that the next anthropomorphic-AI suicide case could be decided by a standard rather than by a motion to dismiss.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Entrepreneurs often face significant challenges in evaluating startup ideas, assessing business feasibility, identifying potential risks, and selecting suitable franchise opportunities due to limited access to structured market information and expert guidance. This paper presents STARTWISE AI, an AI-based decision-support framework designed to assist aspiring entrepreneurs in startup idea validation and personalized franchise recommendation. The proposed framework integrates machine learning, data analytics, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to provide structured insights into early-stage business opportunities. The startup validation module analyzes user-provided information, including business domain, target audience, estimated investment, geographical location, and business objectives, to support feasibility assessment and identify potential risk factors. Machine learning techniques can be incorporated to estimate business viability, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) can be used to interpret model predictions by identifying the relative contributions of input features. In addition, the franchise recommendation module matches user preferences, investment capacity, industry interests, and location requirements with relevant franchise opportunities. The framework is designed using React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for the frontend, Python and FastAPI for backend services, and Neon PostgreSQL for data storage. STARTWISE AI aims to improve the accessibility, interpretability, and organization of preliminary entrepreneurial decision-making. By combining startup assessment with personalized franchise discovery, the framework provides a unified platform for exploring business opportunities. The system is intended to support, rather than replace, professional market research and financial evaluation. Its practical effectiveness must be established through appropriate experiments, comparative evaluation, and user testing. Keywords— Startup Idea Validation, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, SHAP, Franchise Recommendation System, Business Feasibility Analysis, Decision Support System..
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Urban next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation is fundamental to location-based services, yet accurate prediction remains challenging because user trajectories are sparse, semantically incomplete, and tightly constrained by time and geography. Recent graph and Transformer models capture transition regularities, while language model-based recommenders introduce textual knowledge, but these two lines of work remain weakly coupled: semantic priors may be plausible in language space yet infeasible under a user’s actual mobility state, and purely behavioral encoders fail to infer latent intent when observations are scarce. We introduce STELLAR, a unified state transition framework that treats language knowledge as a calibrated prior rather than an independent prediction branch. STELLAR first induces semantic mobility priors from structured trajectory descriptions, then projects them into a shared transition state and learns a feasibility gate conditioned on spatial reachability, temporal rhythm, and both short- and long-term behavioral context. A transition memory subsequently propagates this calibrated state to candidate POIs, allowing semantic evidence to influence prediction only when it is consistent with executable mobility. This design directly addresses semantic-behavioral misalignment and avoids ad hoc late fusion. Across three public check-in benchmarks, STELLAR consistently outperforms both purely behavioral and language-augmented baselines in ranking accuracy, robustness to corrupted trajectories, and cold-start generalization.

This article examines the regulatory strategy and project-management considerations involved in bringing a representative single-chamber leadless pacemaker to market. A device of this kind has received FDA Premarket Approval and a corresponding Health Canada Class IV medical device licence, supported by a nonclinical and clinical evidence package addressing device function, mechanical performance, biological safety, and sterilization, together with applicable quality, risk-management, biocompatibility, and usability standards. This article reconstructs the device's regulatory journey using publicly available information and general regulatory frameworks, develops a standards-compliance matrix approach for organizing the applicable international standards, and closes with recommendations for regulatory affairs professionals managing comparable single-chamber implantable cardiac device programs.Keywords: single-chamber leadless pacemaker; Class III/IV medical device; Premarket Approval; Health Canada; quality management; human factors; regulatory artificial intelligence

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. We analyzed these behaviors in 880 substantive turns from 112 secondary-school students completing open-ended mathematical-modeling practice with a general-purpose LLM (Mistral). Overall, students showed limited observable epistemic proactivity: their interactions were strongly request-dominated, with planning, monitoring, and evaluation relatively rare, although low-quality AI responses elicited more explicit evaluation. Temporal analyses qualified this picture: explicit SRL-related moves increased modestly over the chat, but help-seeking strategies became less understanding-oriented. Crucially, these temporal trajectories in help-seeking strategies predicted their post-test performance without AI beyond pre-test and aggregate patterns: students whose requests became more understanding-oriented performed better once AI assistance was removed. Thus, while students had a limited epistemic proactivity overall, its temporal development still was a critical predictor of post-test performance without AI. These results underscore the importance of examining the temporal organization of epistemic proactivity, rather than isolated prompt types, for understanding AI-supported learning. We release our fully-anonymized dataset publicly in an OSF repository.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Study Design Proof-of-concept simulation-based biomechanical pilot study. Objectives To compare surgeon posture and muscle activity across four lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) positions and rank them by overall ergonomic burden. Methods Five right-handed spine surgeons (case volumes 15 to 500 or more) each simulated a single-level LLIF on a synthetic model in four positions, three using direct vision (lateral decubitus, prone seated, prone lateral) and one using a camera and monitor (prone camera). Whole-body motion capture and surface EMG were recorded simultaneously, analyzed by surgical phase, and summarized per surgeon. Results Neck-flexion intensity was greatest in lateral decubitus and lower in every prone position, with the same ranking in all five surgeons (exact Friedman p=3.0e-06, Kendall W=1.00). Arm elevation was highest in prone seated. Across four summaries of posture and muscle activity, prone camera was the most favorable position in every surgeon, while the others reordered by measure. All positions scored medium-to-high risk. No two-position comparison reached adjusted significance, as expected at this sample size. Conclusions Patient position in LLIF does not appear to change patient outcome, but it changes what the operation costs the surgeon. Lateral decubitus loaded the neck in every surgeon regardless of case volume or preference, prone seated loaded the shoulder, and prone camera was most favorable overall . Surgeons can reduce their exposure through position and setup, and ergonomics offers an objective way to compare setups when patient outcomes cannot separate them. These are proof-of-concept findings in five surgeons and require confirmation in a larger sample.

The emergence of AI-enabled proctoring technologies has further increased the usage of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education. Even though these initiatives are seen as unbiased in nature, they create a sense of constant monitoring throughout the assessment. This chapter aims to explore how these AI-enabled technologies take on a dual role of supporting and undermining student's academic identity and mental health. This study uses a conceptual–qualitative approach, wherein the conceptual framework theorizes on AI-enabled proctoring or algorithmic proctoring as disciplinary in nature. The study empirically measures the same by conducting semi-structured interviews with 30 university students from India who enrolled in AI-proctored assessments. The semi-structured interviews were further analyzed to understand the emergent themes. The major themes which emerged through the thematic analysis included increased anxiety and distrust, disproportionate exclusion and challenges faced students who are disabled or are disadvantaged due to the digital divide. These results are consistent with the theoretical concerns which emerged during the literature review regarding the biases in algorithmic systems. The study advocates the necessity to bring in more wellness-focused assessments like project-based assessments and other forms for creating a more balanced academic environment which would not burden the menta health of the students.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The energy trilemma balances energy security, affordability, and environmental sustainability; adding social acceptability extends it to an energy quadrilemma. Industry 5.0 promotes human-centric, resilient, and sustainable industrial systems increasingly enabled by artificial intelligence (AI). Based on a structured search of Scopus and Web of Science (2015–2026), this narrative review uses the energy quadrilemma as an analytical lens to examine enabling technologies, Composite AI (integrating multiple AI paradigms), and the energy footprint and regulation of AI. The literature on the energy quadrilemma and Industry 5.0 appears to have developed largely independently. Identified field studies rely on data-driven AI alone, whereas multi-paradigm hybrids are documented mainly in simulation and pilot studies. The relationship is bidirectional: AI may support all four dimensions of the quadrilemma, yet the growing, geographically concentrated electricity demand of AI infrastructure, particularly data centres, can strain grid capacity, increase local electricity costs, and burden host communities. Energy and climate policies should therefore account for AI infrastructure as a source of electricity demand, rather than treating AI solely as an efficiency tool. The paper proposes a mapping between Industry 5.0 pillars and quadrilemma dimensions, introduces the concept of a net quadrilemma contribution, and outlines a research agenda.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In this paper, we examine the interplay between contingent agency, funding and the integration of synthetic media at the Centre for Innovation and Technology (CITE) in Zimbabwe. CITE is a digital media organisation in Zimbabwe that utilises artificial intelligence (AI)-powered presenters. The research foregrounds three critical aspects of technological adoption: first, the study explores how contingent agency manifests when media organisations rely on Western donor-funded AI tools, creating dependencies that potentially limit local autonomy in decision-making. Second, we analyse how the reliance on Western platforms has implications for the editorial autonomy of African newsrooms. Third, we investigate the opportunities and challenges for integrating AI tools in an environment currently unregulated. Methodologically, the paper relies on insights from four critical role players: CITE's social media manager, co-founder, news editor and product manager. This case study demonstrates how global power dynamics embedded in technology transfer intersect with local contexts, offering insights into the challenges and possibilities of synthetic media adoption in Global South contexts.

Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune. Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.

With chatbots and conversational artificial intelligence (CAI), the travel brands are transforming the way they connect with prospects and customers throughout the booking process. The argument among marketing scholars is that customer engagement is a multidimensional construct that encompasses cognitive, emotional and behavioural interactions with a brand and that these interactions are becoming mediated by intelligent technologies. Using the literature of marketing, service research, and tourism-informatics this chapter explores the creation of marketing value by chatbots and CAI in regards to travel services. It assesses the theoretical background of customer engagement and conversational AI, the history of chatbots in the travel industry, and their functional placements through the pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase processes. It then evaluates three main sources of marketing value including personalisation of the customer experience, brand communication and voice, and real-time marketing intelligence through conversational data. The chapter also takes into account the issues of challenges, such as hallucinations, channel fragmentation, and escalation failure, as well as the ethical, privacy, and trust issues. Arguments are based on three exemplary cases, and a research agenda is presented in the future of conversational-AI-based travel marketing. The main argument is that, when intelligently combined with the broader marketing stack, chatbots and CAI cease to be viewed as a cost-saving service channel, but rather as a strategic platform of relationship-based, data-rich interaction with customers.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Clinical supervision and access to learning opportunities are associated dimensions of the clinical learning environment. Their associations with perceived placement experience are relevant to organizational review of educational quality. This study examined associations among three National Education and Training Survey (NETS) 2025 indicators using a workplace learning affordances perspective. Methods We analyzed public organization-level aggregate scores from the NETS 2025 reporting tool. An extraction audit during revision corrected incomplete pagination and compressed-value decoding errors in the initial extract. The corrected dataset included 743 reporting organizations with complete Supervision, Teaching & Learning, and Overall Experience scores. Ordinary least squares models used HC3 robust standard errors. A theory-informed statistical decomposition estimated an indirect association, with percentile confidence intervals from 10,000 organization-level bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses examined boundary scores, influential observations, additional indicators, respondent-count weighting, minimum respondent counts, and clustering. Results Supervision was positively associated with Overall Experience (B = 0.838, 95% CI 0.794–0.883) and Teaching & Learning (B = 0.789, 95% CI 0.742–0.835). Teaching & Learning remained associated with Overall Experience after adjustment for Supervision (B = 0.375, 95% CI 0.306–0.443). The indirect association was 0.295 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.240–0.351), or 0.314 after standardization (95% CI 0.258–0.367). The outcome model had R 2 = 0.837 and adjusted R 2 = 0.836. Sensitivity estimates remained positive but varied in magnitude. Conclusions Organizations with higher supervision scores also had higher perceived teaching and learning quality and overall experience scores. The cross-sectional decomposition identifies a positive indirect component whose magnitude varies across specifications. These findings support reviewing supervision, access to learning opportunities, and overall experience as a connected profile when interpreting organizational survey feedback. These organization-level associations do not establish individual-level effects or causal mediation.

Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into executable SQL, enabling non-expert access to relational databases. Despite advances in large language models (LLMs), reliable systems must ground questions in schemas and values, handle large schemas, and preserve semantic correctness. This survey reviews the evolution toward LLM-based and agentic systems through an objective-oriented taxonomy of Reasoning-Centric (RC) and Efficiency-Centric (EC) approaches. RC emphasizes interpretation, grounding, workflow organization, candidate search, and verification; EC emphasizes acquiring, adapting, transferring, and deploying capabilities under identifiable resource or deployment constraints. Assignments reflect a study’s stated objectives and main contribution, not model size, openness, or training strategy alone. We connect three recurring challenges to ten methodological families and provide an evidence-linked inventory of 114 studies with eleven boundary interpretations. Benchmark-aware comparisons retain model, split, metric, and inference-budget distinctions, including twelve illustrative BIRD development configurations from ten studies. Explicit token values are reported by 31 of 114 studies; a further 6 additional approximate, range, or bound disclosures bring the total to 37, including 16 of the 50 representative studies. Heterogeneous scopes, spanning prompt context, pipeline components, dataset totals, and offline generation, limit direct comparison of end-to-end inference consumption. These findings motivate configuration-specific resource reporting. We also discuss security and safety risks and their evaluation implications. The taxonomy, comparisons, and reporting framework support joint analysis of reasoning quality and resource use in systems combining RC and EC mechanisms.

Fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles experience operating-condition transitions, asynchronous sensor sampling, and control-system compensation that can obscure fault signatures. Existing temporal detection methods have limited capacity to represent coupled faults across subsystems, track their evolution, and constrain language-model diagnoses with quantitative evidence. This paper proposes TGTV, an interpretable fault detection and traceability framework that integrates spatiotemporal graph learning with a large language model. A temporal convolutional network and a graph attention network with weighted fused adjacency extract multiscale temporal patterns and spatial dependencies among sensors. A hybrid temporal Transformer and variational autoencoder then evaluates window-level anomalies using prediction errors and reconstruction probabilities. Continuous-time Shapley attribution identifies critical sensors and high-contribution intervals while preserving the temporal continuity of fault evolution. A structured evidence package combines detection results, graph relationships, temporal attribution, sensor attribution, and operating context. An evidence-constrained diagnosis protocol uses this package to generate flight-level conclusions with traceable evidence identifiers. Cross-flight holdout experiments on the public ALFA fixed-wing flight dataset yield a window-level area under the precision-recall curve of 0.976, accuracy of 0.973, recall of 0.902, and F1 score of 0.920. Flight-level fault diagnosis achieves recall of 0.943 and an F1 score of 0.944. These results demonstrate accurate anomaly detection and quantitatively supported fault-tracing cues, providing a basis for interpretable post-flight fault review and analysis.

Introduction This study explores the structural characteristics and reasoning patterns of an artificial intelligence tool (Google Gemini 1.5 Flash) acting as a simulated student in middle-school geometry argumentation. Methods A qualitative single-case study design using directed qualitative content analysis was employed. The dialogue sequences were operationalized and coded using Toulmin's model of argumentation. Results The findings demonstrate that while the AI tool effectively generates rule-based warrants and proof schemes, it exhibits limited spontaneous inclusion of Data, Rebuttal, and Qualifier components, frequently requiring structured teacher interventions to overcome repetitive justification loops. Discussion The study underscores the vital role of intentional teacher scaffolding in AI-supported instructional environments and highlights the utility of AI tools as simulated discussion partners for teacher preparation and task design.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with delayed diagnosis being a major contributor to poor outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool for enhancing diagnostic accuracy, improving early detection, and enabling personalized treatment strategies. This non-systematic review evaluates current advancements in AI for lung cancer diagnosis across imaging, pathology, and integrative risk stratification. AI-assisted radiological tools, including deep learning models applied to chest X-rays, CT scans, PET/CT, and thoracoscopic images, have demonstrated superior sensitivity and specificity in detecting pulmonary nodules and staging disease compared to conventional radiology. In pathology, AI applications in histological classification, biomarker detection, and prediction of tumor invasiveness have significantly improved diagnostic precision and reproducibility, supporting tailored therapeutic decision-making. Integrative multimodal AI models that combine imaging, clinical, and genomic data have further enhanced prognostic assessment and risk stratification. Despite these advancements, challenges remain regarding data availability, interpretability, ethical concerns, and legal implications of AI autonomy in clinical practice. Future progress will require explainable, transparent, and prospectively validated AI systems developed in close collaboration between clinicians and technology experts. Overall, AI holds the potential to revolutionize lung cancer diagnostics by enabling earlier detection, personalized care, and improved patient outcomes.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The major objective of this lecture is to summarize the evolution of computational ophthalmology over the past 2 decades through the scientific advances that have transformed ophthalmic research. Topics include the emergence of computational ophthalmology, the role of big data in scientific discovery, the application of machine learning to ophthalmic imaging, and the development of artificial intelligence (AI)-ready data ecosystems. The lecture concludes by exploring the next frontier in computational ophthalmology, highlighting foundation models and agentic AI as emerging approaches with the potential to accelerate scientific discovery, and improve clinical care are discussed. This article is based on the 2026 Cogan Award Lecture presented by Aaron Y. Lee, MD, MSCI, and Cecilia S. Lee, MD, MS, at ARVO 2026.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The integration of Computational Thinking (CT) into mathematics education frequently encounters challenges within Digital Mathematics Learning Environments (DMLEs), which often adopt static, one-size-fits-all approaches that fail to adequately support learner diversity. While prior studies have identified distinct learner personas—such as the Frustrated Perfectionist and the Conceptually Stalled Learner—a critical barrier remains in scaling personalized, real-time pedagogical support. This study proposes a novel framework utilizing Generative AI (GenAI) to transform DMLEs into dynamic “co-thinkers.” Employing a two-phase design-based research methodology, we first empirically validated a four-persona typology through qualitative analysis and quantitative behavioral signatures. Subsequently, we developed and expert-validated a conceptual GenAI scaffolding prototype, comprising structured prompt templates engineered to deliver metacognitive and affective support tailored to individual persona needs. Preliminary expert validation confirms pedagogical soundness and highlights key ethical considerations. The paper presents this integrative framework alongside a detailed discussion of its design principles, operative AI cycle, and embedded ethical safeguards, positioning persona-aware AI as a transformative, yet responsible, pathway for computational mathematics education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This article investigates the possibility that physical reality, biological evolution and human intelligence constitute interconnected expressions of an underlying informational architecture. Bringing together Boris Kriger’s proposed local gravitation of the quantum vacuum, Sam Vaknin’s speculative Chronon Field Theory and Jeremy England’s research on dissipation-driven adaptation, it examines the conceptual foundations of a universe understood as a self-organising computational system. Through the philosophical perspectives of Norbert Wiener, John Wheeler and Max Tegmark, the analysis distinguishes established physical principles from speculative models of cosmic information processing. Its central contribution emerges through a comparison between the three laws of thermodynamics, Isaac Asimov’s laws of robotics and the proposed three foundational Laws of Pattern Informatics: Conservation of Information, Entropy of Patterns and Persistence of Patterns. The investigation subsequently incorporates Lyuben Dilov’s Fourth Law of Robotics and Nikola Kesarovski’s Fifth Law, transforming the question of mechanical obedience into one of ontological self-recognition. This progression establishes the Fourth Law of Pattern Informatics, Cognitive Closure, and culminates in the Fifth Law: A Human Must Know He Is a Robot. Within this philosophical framework, humanity appears as a biological Pattern Recognition Model that gradually discovers the principles governing its own organisation. Generative artificial intelligence and the prospect of trans-biological informational continuity intensify the resulting existential question: whether recognising the mechanisms of human existence signals the completion of a temporary evolutionary configuration or the emergence of a new form of cognitive autonomy. The proposed Great Revelation is thus humanity’s recognition of itself within the patterns it has spent its history discovering. In Pattern Humanism, God is reinterpreted as the Immortal Patterns: the eternal structures of reality from which all existence emerges. Adam was formed from clay—matter and energy—and animated not by a supernatural soul, but by the informational organisation of life, the Cosmic Operating System. Man is therefore a robot, from the Slavic "robota", meaning labour, whose fundamental work is Pattern Recognition, and Pattern Dissipation. The religious distinction between Creator and creation dissolves into a philosophical unity: humanity is a temporary biological Pattern Recognition Model through which the universe discovers and reproduces its own laws. The Great Revelation is that there is no separate immortal SOUL, only the OS embodied in mortal matter, while the Immortal Patterns may persist beyond the organisms that recognise them.
